proposedTopics.title: Types & layout gas
proposedTopics.description: The EVM is a 256-bit machine, so type and data-structure choices have non-obvious gas effects: smaller types can cost more when they do not reduce storage slots, bitmaps compact indexed flags, and mappings suit keyed access.

proposedTopics.title: Assembly & Yul gas
proposedTopics.description: Inline assembly exposes EVM operations and memory or storage locations directly. It can remove work on measured hot paths, but the author must preserve Solidity's memory, type-cleaning, call-failure, and storage-layout invariants.

proposedTopics.title: Architecture-level gas
proposedTopics.description: The biggest wins can be structural: deploy clones instead of full contracts, share a singleton where its coupling is acceptable, batch calls, verify compact off-chain commitments, and use withdrawal-based payments to isolate recipients.

proposedTopics.title: Word-size choices
proposedTopics.description: The EVM operates on 256-bit words. A narrow integer only saves storage gas when layout packing reduces the number of slots; otherwise Solidity may need extra operations to clean or mask it. Treat `uint256` as the baseline for standalone arithmetic and loop counters, use narrow storage fields deliberately for packing, and compare optimized bytecode or gas measurements instead of assuming the type name determines cost.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/WordSize.sol — compare optimized `uint8` and `uint256` standalone counters, then pack two narrow storage fields and explain the different result. Done when: forge test passes and forge snapshot records both comparisons without assuming a compiler-independent numeric threshold.

proposedTopics.title: bytes32 over string
proposedTopics.description: A `bytes32` value is a fixed-size value type with direct equality and no runtime length. Solidity packs a `string` or `bytes` value of at most 31 bytes together with its encoded length in one storage slot, while longer values use a length marker plus data starting at a hashed location. Use `bytes32` for truly fixed, byte-oriented identifiers; use `string` for variable-length UTF-8 text. The short forms may occupy the same number of storage slots, so measure the operations that matter.

Done when: forge test passes, snapshot results are recorded, and the explanation notes that both short values can occupy one storage slot while their operations differ.

proposedTopics.title: Bitmaps for boolean flags
proposedTopics.description: A bitmap addresses 256 indexed flags inside each `uint256` storage word. It is especially compact compared with `mapping(uint256 => bool)`, whose independently hashed entries occupy distinct slots; contiguous declared `bool` fields and array elements may already be packed by Solidity. Bitmap updates still perform a read-modify-write on the containing word, so the saving depends on flag density and access patterns.

proposedTopics.title: Mappings vs arrays
proposedTopics.description: Mappings provide direct keyed access but have no length, key set, or enumeration order. Dynamic arrays provide indexed access, length, ordering, and iteration; `push` updates their length, while indexed reads are also constant-time rather than linear scans. Choose by required semantics: use a mapping for a known key, an array for ordered enumeration, or both only when the product needs both capabilities.

proposedTopics.title: Cheap hashing in assembly
proposedTopics.description: For two full-word values, inline assembly can write at `0x00` and `0x20` and hash the 64-byte scratch region with `keccak256(0x00, 0x40)`, avoiding a separate ABI-encoded dynamic object. Solidity reserves `0x00`–`0x3f` as scratch space between statements and stores the free-memory pointer at `0x40`; code must not overwrite memory outside the promised region or rely on scratch contents surviving another statement.
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: solve gas/AsmHash.sol — compute `keccak256(abi.encode(a, b))` equivalently from the 64-byte scratch region. Done when: forge test compares hashes across fuzzed words, a memory-safety test preserves the free-memory pointer, and forge snapshot records rather than presupposes the compiler-dependent delta.

proposedTopics.title: Direct storage slots in assembly
proposedTopics.description: Inline assembly can read and write an explicitly chosen storage slot with `sload` and `sstore`, outside Solidity's declared-variable layout. ERC-7201 standardizes NatSpec annotations and the formula `keccak256(keccak256(id) - 1) & ~0xff` for aligned namespaced roots. A wrong or overlapping slot silently corrupts unrelated state, so use a specified layout formula, inspect compiler storage layout, and test collision boundaries.

proposedTopics.title: Low-level calls in Yul
proposedTopics.description: Yul exposes `call`, `staticcall`, and `delegatecall` directly, including input/output memory regions, forwarded gas, value, and the success flag. This control can avoid unused return-data handling on a measured path, but it also removes Solidity's typed return decoding and automatic failure behavior. Correct code checks success, copies and bubbles revert data when required, validates any expected return shape, and treats calls to addresses without code according to the application's contract.

proposedTopics.title: Bit masking
proposedTopics.description: Shift a packed field down and apply a width-accurate mask to extract it; clear that field's mask and OR a bounded replacement to update it without changing neighbors. Solidity does not guarantee that high bits outside a narrow type are clean in every assembly-visible context, so mask narrow values before depending on them. The same operations are available in Solidity itself; assembly is warranted only when measurement and layout control justify it.

Done when: boundary and fuzz tests prove neighboring fields are unchanged and oversized input cannot leak into them; forge snapshot compares Solidity and assembly implementations without a fixed threshold.

proposedTopics.title: Function selector optimization
proposedTopics.description: An external function selector is the first four bytes of the Keccak-256 hash of its canonical signature, and compiler-generated dispatch code routes calldata by that selector. Selector value alone does not create a portable source-level gas guarantee: dispatch structure can change with compiler version, optimizer pipeline, and interface size. Mine or rename selectors only after inspecting the exact compiled bytecode and benchmarking a genuinely hot entrypoint, while preserving ABI and readability costs.

proposedTopics.title: Minimal-proxy clones for gas (EIP-1167)
proposedTopics.description: ERC-1167 standardizes a minimal 45-byte runtime proxy that delegates calls to one fixed implementation and returns or reverts with its returndata. Clones avoid redeploying the implementation bytecode for every instance, but each call pays delegation overhead and executes against the clone's storage. Per-instance state therefore needs a protected initializer or immutable-arguments design rather than the implementation's constructor.

proposedTopics.title: Singleton contracts
proposedTopics.description: A singleton can hold many logical instances behind one deployed contract, keyed by an identifier rather than one address per instance. Uniswap v4's PoolManager uses this architecture for pools and supports flash accounting across actions. It removes repeated deployments and can share warmed state, but concentrates trust, upgrade, accounting, and access-control boundaries; choose it for cross-instance benefits, not as a universal replacement for isolated contracts.

proposedTopics.title: Batching and multicall
proposedTopics.description: A batch entrypoint or multicall amortizes per-transaction intrinsic gas across several operations. Within one transaction, later accesses to the same account or storage key use the warm-access schedule introduced by EIP-2929. The batch still pays loop, calldata, and dispatch costs, and its atomicity must be explicit: either bubble a failure and revert the whole batch or deliberately represent per-item results.

proposedTopics.title: Pull over push payments
proposedTopics.description: A push loop invokes every recipient during distribution, grows with recipient count, and can let one reverting recipient block an atomic batch. The withdrawal pattern records each recipient's credit and lets recipients claim separately, isolating external calls and moving withdrawal gas to each claimer. Crediting N recipients still requires N accounting updates unless a compact commitment is used, and withdrawal must zero credit before the external call to prevent reentrancy.

Done when: tests prove one reverting recipient cannot block others, credit is cleared before interaction, reentrancy cannot double-withdraw, and snapshot compares distribution and per-recipient withdrawal without an impossible 30000-gas cap for five fresh credits.

proposedTopics.title: Off-chain compute, on-chain verify
proposedTopics.description: A contract can verify an off-chain commitment instead of storing or recomputing the full dataset. A Merkle root commits to leaves and an inclusion proof supplies a logarithmic hash path; EIP-712 signs typed structured data bound to a domain. These tools reduce some on-chain state or computation but introduce proof construction, replay protection, leaf-encoding, trusted-input, and data-availability responsibilities; they do not make every verification cheaper than a direct lookup.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why can a standalone `uint8` cost more gas than a `uint256`?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The EVM works on 256-bit words, so a narrow unpacked type may require cleanup without reducing storage slots. Pitfall: optimizer results vary — use uint256 as a baseline, pack narrow storage fields deliberately, and measure the exact build.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the cheaper type choice for a standalone counter and say why.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: uint256 i; // full-word baseline; compile and measure against uint8 because optimizer output, not the spelling alone, decides the result.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When is bytes32 a better fit than string, and what storage misconception should you avoid?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 is a fixed value type with direct equality; a short string of at most 31 bytes also packs data and length into one slot, while longer strings spill to hashed storage. Choose bytes32 for fixed byte-oriented data, not variable UTF-8 text, and measure the operations instead of assuming a short string always takes more slots.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a mapping from a bytes32 key to a value instead of a string key.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: mapping(bytes32 => uint256) public byKey; // fixed-size key with direct value semantics; use string only when variable UTF-8 identity is required.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How can a bitmap compact 256 keyed bool mapping entries, and what's the cost?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Each word addresses 256 indexed flags, so dense mapping-bool entries can share storage. Each update still read-modify-writes the containing word. Cost: shift/mask arithmetic; pitfall: declared bool fields and array elements may already pack, and boundary bugs can corrupt neighboring flags.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write set-bit and test-bit for a uint256 bitmap `bits` at index i (i < 256).
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bits |= (1 << i);  // set   bool isSet = ((bits >> i) & 1) == 1; // test; parentheses avoid equality-precedence ambiguity

proposedPrompts.promptText: When is a mapping cheaper than an array, and when do you still need an array?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Mapping: direct access for a known key but no length or enumeration. Array: direct numeric indexing plus length/order/iteration. Pitfall: arrays are not inherently linear-time — only an application-level search is; keep both structures only if both semantics are required.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a keyed record store using a mapping instead of a scanned array.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: mapping(uint256 => Record) public records; // O(1) records[id] lookup vs an O(n) array scan.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do you compute a mapping slot's keccak256 cheaply in assembly?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Write key and slot to scratch space (0x00 and 0x20) and call keccak256(0x00, 0x40) — skips abi.encode's memory allocation; keccak is 30 + 6/word. Pitfall: don't overflow past 0x40 into the free-memory area or you corrupt it.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly that hashes two 32-byte words via scratch space.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { mstore(0x00, a) mstore(0x20, b) let h := keccak256(0x00, 0x40) }

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why use sload/sstore on a fixed slot, and how do you avoid collisions?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Fixed-slot assembly supports specified layouts such as ERC-7201. For ERC-7201 use keccak256(keccak256(id) - 1) & ~0xff and annotate the namespace. Pitfall: a wrong or overlapping slot silently corrupts unrelated storage.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly to read and write a value at a fixed namespaced slot.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 slot = keccak256(abi.encode(uint256(keccak256(bytes("my.namespace"))) - 1)) & ~bytes32(uint256(0xff)); assembly { let v := sload(slot) sstore(slot, add(v, 1)) } // a production constant can use the precomputed audited value

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does calling in Yul save, and what must you handle yourself?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It controls gas, value, and input/output memory directly and can avoid copying return data you truly do not need. You must check success, bubble or interpret returndata, validate expected return shape, and define no-code-target behavior yourself.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a Yul call that reverts if the callee fails.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { let ok := call(gas(), target, 0, add(data,0x20), mload(data), 0, 0) if iszero(ok) { returndatacopy(0,0,returndatasize()) revert(0, returndatasize()) } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: How do you read one packed field out of a slot with shift and mask?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Shift the field down (shr) then AND with a mask sized exactly to the field (e.g. 0xff for 8 bits). Pitfall: a mask wider than the field reads neighboring bits — match the mask to the field width exactly.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write assembly to extract the low byte of a word `x`.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: assembly { let b := and(x, 0xff) } // isolates bits 0–7; use shr first to read a higher field.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How can function naming reduce dispatch gas?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A suffix changes keccak256(canonicalSignature) and therefore the selector, which may alter the exact compiled dispatcher. There is no portable low-selector-first guarantee: inspect bytecode and benchmark the pinned compiler/optimizer, then weigh the ABI/readability cost.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Show how a mined name suffix changes a function's selector.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes4 sel = bytes4(keccak256("transfer_hot(address,uint256)")); // proves the selector changed; inspect the compiled dispatcher before claiming it routes earlier.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is deploying an EIP-1167 clone so much cheaper than a full contract?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A clone has a 45-byte runtime that delegatecalls shared implementation code, avoiding redeploying that full runtime per instance. Pitfall: deployment is not merely a few thousand gas; initialize clone storage exactly once and measure delegation overhead too.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a clone-factory deploy using OpenZeppelin Clones.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: address c = Clones.clone(implementation); IInit(c).initialize(args); // compare total clone+initialization gas with `new Impl()` and guard re-initialization.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a singleton architecture cut gas versus a contract per instance?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: One deployed contract holds all instances keyed by id, as Uniswap v4's PoolManager does for pools, removing per-instance deploy cost and enabling shared optimizations like transient flash accounting. Pitfall: one contract mediating all instances, concentrating risk and complicating access control.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a singleton state layout keyed by an instance id.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: mapping(bytes32 => Pool) internal pools; // one contract, per-id state, no per-instance deployment.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What costs does batching many operations into one tx amortize?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It amortizes intrinsic transaction gas; repeated accesses to the same account/key later in that transaction can also be warm. Pitfall: define failure atomicity plus msg.sender and msg.value semantics — silent skips hide failures.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write a multicall that executes an array of encoded self-calls.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function multicall(bytes[] calldata calls) external { for (uint256 i; i < calls.length;) { (bool ok,) = address(this).delegatecall(calls[i]); require(ok); unchecked { ++i; } } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does pull-payment isolate recipient failures and shift gas compared with pushing in a loop?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Push loops make recipient calls during distribution and one revert can block an atomic batch. Pull records each credit, then each claimant pays for an isolated withdrawal. It is not a universal total-gas saving: N credits still need N accounting updates; clear credit before the external call.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write credit-then-withdraw functions replacing a push loop.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function credit(address u, uint256 a) internal { owed[u] += a; } function withdraw() external { uint256 a = owed[msg.sender]; owed[msg.sender] = 0; (bool ok,) = payable(msg.sender).call{value:a}(""); require(ok); } // CEI; add a reentrancy guard when surrounding state needs it.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a merkle airdrop save gas over storing every claim on-chain?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Store only a 32-byte root; each claimant submits an ~log(n)-hash proof the contract verifies, instead of an SSTORE-set per eligible address at setup. Pitfall: still track claimed status (a bitmap) so a valid proof can't be replayed.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write the on-chain verify step for a merkle-proof-gated claim.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: bytes32 leaf = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, amount)); require(MerkleProof.verify(proof, root, leaf)); // then mark claimed in a bitmap.
